title: A Tiny Detail
reviewNotes: Montages, captions and native complete diagrams reviewed. Native47 confirms the complete twelve-piece final correct-order board after Kh2: White Kh2/Qe8/Be4/a2/b2/f2 against Kg4/Re1/Nb4/Nf4/a5/c7, Black to move. Independent Rxe4/Qxe4 removes both bishop and rook, leaving TEN pieces, correcting the earlier note that said eleven; old draft/history remain preserved. Independent Re2/Qg8+/Ng6 shows a legal rook move, queen check and knight interposition. Re2 itself is not check because White f2 blocks the second rank. Neither comparison is a recovered game continuation or exact conversion proof. Verify every Black rook/knight reply and the resulting larger queen ending. The separate premature-f3/Kh4 diagram and source move-order comparisons remain preserved and must not be spliced into this f2/Kg4 board. Source images/captions are available; no new missing-information claim is made.
transcript: Sometimes the difference between a win and a loss lies in the tiniest [music] of details. And that is exactly the case with this position. White is only one step away from promoting this pawn. But unfortunately, the rook is simply going to be able to stop it. Sacrificing the bishop to defend the queening square doesn't work because the rook can simply take the pawn and ignore the bishop. And it's going to take this rook way too many moves to come and help the pawn. So, it seems like black is simply winning in this position, right? Well, not exactly. White has an incredible move in this position, the beautiful rook E1. Of course, this move is defending the pawn with an X-ray across the black rook. But naturally, we can see [music] that this rook is also hanging to rook takes C1. And now the black rook is still defending the pawn. But believe it or not, finding the sacrifice with rook E1 was not the hardest part of this position. Because now some of you might think that the idea is to go F3 check, force the king to move, and then play bishop E4 and cut the communication of the rook with the pawn, allowing us to promote on the next move. But believe it or not, after F3 check, there is no way to win for white after the surprising king H4. If we now play bishop E4, preparing to promote, black has the incredible knight d5, we get a queen. And it seems like we're completely winning. But there is a surprise coming with knight to f4 check. Now it's white that needs to be careful because after king f2, we are actually losing to knight d3 check. This is almost checkmate around this king, meaning that we have to take the knight. And now after this check, we're also going to lose the queen. end the game. And if the king goes to H2 now, at the very least, black has a perpetual check with the rook and there is going to be no way to make any progress. So, if we go back to this position, believe it or not, the only way to win this for white is to change the order of the moves and play bishop to E4 first, sacrificing the bishop completely. But, of course, if this bishop is taken now, we're going to be able to follow up with F3 with a fork. The king has to move. We pick up the rook. And now we're simply going to promote. And if black ignores us and tries to prepare the same attack with knight to d5, now we can simply get a queen. And because we have not spent an extra move on f3 after knight to f4 check, we can go to h2 [music] and be shielded by the rook checks. And now white will be able to win this game.
